items: Read stdin or file args, write stdout, errors to stderr
That one uniform contract is what makes chaining possible
grep selects lines; sed edits lines; awk computes on fields
cut slices columns; sort orders; uniq collapses ADJACENT dupes
A text file is a byte stream split on \n
POSIX: a line ENDS with \n, so a file missing it is malformed
Most tools still process that last line; some silently drop it
Streaming = constant memory, one line held at a time

lines: grep ERROR huge.log   # fine on a 500 GB file
cmd1 | cmd2           # kernel pipe buf ~64 KB
# both processes run CONCURRENTLY, not in turn

blocks.title: Buffering Trap
items: stdout is line-buffered to a TTY
block-buffered (4-8 KB) into a pipe
`tail -f log | grep X | tee out` stalls
Fix: `grep --line-buffered` or `stdbuf -oL`

lines: grep -q pat file && echo yes  # the idiom
yes | head -1        # yes gets SIGPIPE, dies

items: `>` writes to a file, `|` writes to a process
`>` truncates BEFORE cmd runs: `sort f > f` destroys f
Filters have no native in-place mode
Use `sed -i`, `cmd f > tmp && mv tmp f`, or `sponge`
BRE: `+ ? { } | ( )` are LITERAL, backslash activates them
ERE: same chars are meta, backslash makes them literal
Exactly inverted — the single biggest source of grep pain

lines: # cut can do neither of these
grep    'a\+'   # BRE: one or more a
grep -E 'a\+'   # ERE: a literal plus sign
# guard n>0 or empty input divides by zero

items: `^` is special only at the START of a BRE, literal elsewhere
Alternation: ERE `cat|dog`, BRE `cat\|dog` (GNU extension)
Groups + backrefs: `\(ab\)\1` in BRE, `(ab)\1` in ERE

blocks.title: Backrefs Are Not Free
blocks.text: Backreferences make matching non-regular — worst case exponential. Keep them out of hot loops.

blocks.title: POSIX Bracket Classes
items: Live inside `[]`, and are locale-aware
`[[:digit:]] [[:alpha:]] [[:space:]]`
`[[:alnum:]] [[:punct:]] [[:upper:]]`
Metacharacters go quiet: `[.*+]` matches literal . * +
To include `]`, put it FIRST: `[]a]`
To include `-`, put it LAST: `[a-]`
`^` first negates the whole class

blocks.title: Greediness Is Leftmost-Longest
items: `<.*>` on `<a><b>` eats the WHOLE string
Fix with a negated class `<[^>]*>` — portable
Lazy `.*?` exists only in PCRE (`grep -P`)
\b \w \s are GNU-only: they fail on BSD/macOS

blocks.title: Always Single-Quote
blocks.text: Double quotes let the shell eat `$`, backticks and `\` before grep ever sees them. Write `grep '$foo\|bar'`.

items: `-q` exits at first match, prints nothing — for `if` tests
Never use `-q` with a pipe you need output from
`-e pat` allows several patterns, or ones starting with `-`
`-f file` reads one pattern per line from a file
`-F -f wordlist.txt` crushes a 10k-term regex alternation

blocks.title: Three Gotchas
items: `grep -v 'a\|b'` drops lines with a OR b (De Morgan)
Missing file exits 2, so `set -e` dies on an honest miss
Binary files: prints 'Binary file X matches' and stops
Force with `-a`/`--text`, skip them with `-I`
`-A n` after, `-B n` before, `-C n` both sides
Non-adjacent groups split by `--`; kill it with `--no-group-separator`
`-r` recurses a directory, `-R` also follows symlinks
`grep -rn 'TODO' src/` is the daily driver

Lookahead `(?=...)` and lookbehind `(?<=...)`

Result: extraction with no capture-group post-processing

items: Boyer-Moore skips bytes it cannot need
Avoids splitting lines it proves cannot match
`LC_ALL=C grep` skips UTF-8 decode: often 2-10x
ripgrep/ag default to recursive + gitignore, but grep is everywhere
Read one line into the PATTERN SPACE
Run the whole script against it
Auto-print the pattern space, then repeat

No address means every line

items: Chain with `-e 'c1' -e 'c2'`, semicolons, or `'/re/{s/a/b/;d}'`
`-f script.sed` runs a script file
`-i` edits in place; `-i.bak` keeps a backup

blocks.title: Turing-Complete, But Don't
blocks.text: Hold space plus branching (`b`, `t`, `:label`) makes sed Turing-complete. Anything needing that is an awk job.

items: `s/regex/replacement/flags` — FIRST match on each line only
The delimiter is whatever follows `s`
Use `s|/usr/bin|/opt/bin|` or `s#a#b#` for paths
s/// sees only the pattern space, never across lines
`&` means the entire match
GNU case: `\U` upper, `\L` lower until `\E`; `\u`/`\l` next char
`\n` inserts a newline; matching one first needs `N`

rows: replace line / read a file in

blocks.title: Untrusted Input Is A Hazard
blocks.text: A shell variable holding `/` or `&` breaks or rewrites your sed command. Sanitize it, or hand the job to awk.

items: Extracts by byte `-b`, character `-c`, or field `-f`
`-d` takes a SINGLE character; multi-char is awk's job
`--output-delimiter=X` changes the separator on the way out

lines: # cut emits FILE order; reordering needs awk

blocks.title: cut Silently Lies
items: Lines lacking the delimiter print WHOLE by default
`-s` suppresses them — usually what you wanted
cut never collapses repeated delimiters
Two spaces make an empty field: `cut -d' '` is near-always wrong
Space-aligned output: use `awk '{print $2}'` or `tr -s ' '` first
cut has zero quoting awareness
Real CSV with commas inside quotes defeats it
Reach for `csvcut` or python there, not a cleverer cut
tr reads ONLY stdin — it takes no file arguments
`tr '\n' ' '` joins lines into one
`tr ' ' '\n'` splits one word per line
That split is the standard prelude to `sort | uniq -c`

blocks.title: Speed & paste
items: cut and tr run no regex engine at all
On multi-GB files `cut -f1` beats `awk '{print $1}'`
`paste -d, a.txt b.txt` joins files column-wise
`paste -sd,` folds many lines into one joined line
No options means a full-line compare in locale collation order
`-u` dedupes by the sort key, not the whole line
That is a subtle and real difference from `uniq`

lines: sort -k2 f        # field 2 THROUGH end of line

items: `-t` sets the separator; default fields are whitespace runs
Leading blanks belong to the field — use `-b` or the `b` modifier
sort is NOT stable by default; `-s` forces it
Stability matters the moment you chain two sorts

blocks.title: Locale Bites
blocks.text: In en_US.UTF-8 sort ignores punctuation and case in collation. `LC_ALL=C sort` gives byte order: deterministic, and much faster.

items: It must read everything before emitting anything
So it is the memory and latency wall of any pipeline
O(n log n); GNU spills to temp files for inputs over RAM
Tune with `-T dir`, `-S 2G`, `--parallel=N`
uniq collapses only ADJACENT duplicate lines
That is why `sort | uniq` is the canonical pair
Comparing neighbours only: O(n) time, O(1) memory
The sort in front is what costs O(n log n)

lines: # -c prefixes each group with its count

rows: every line of every dup group
nocase / skip fields / chars / compare n

items: `sort -k2 | uniq -f1` treats field 1 (a timestamp) as noise
`sort -u` is faster: dedupes during the merge, less I/O
But `sort -u` cannot count — use `uniq -c` for frequencies
`sort -u -k2,2` keeps an arbitrary representative line
uniq instead compares the TEXT after skipped fields — not the same

blocks.title: Padded Output Bites
blocks.text: `uniq -c` right-aligns and space-pads counts, which breaks naive `cut -d' ' -f1`. Pipe through `awk '{print $1}'` or `sed 's/^ *//'`.

lines: awk '{c[$0]++} END{for(k in c) print c[k], k}'
sort -u f | wc -l        # total distinct count

items: `!seen[$0]++` keeps the FIRST occurrence, O(n) time
Costs O(distinct) memory instead of a full sort
Counting in one pass holds every distinct key in RAM
`awk '!seen[$0]++' f | wc -l` when input order matters
It splits input into RECORDS (lines), records into FIELDS
Then runs every `pattern { action }` rule against each record
Not a command with flags — a pattern-scanning program

rows: record no. overall / within this file

items: Default splits on whitespace RUNS and trims lead/trail blanks
That is why awk survives ragged `ls -l` where cut fails
`-F:` a char, `-F'\t'` a tab, `-F',[ ]*'` a REGEX
FS is a regex once it is longer than one character
`-F''` splits into characters (gawk)

blocks.title: FS=" " Is Magic
blocks.text: The default `FS=" "` means 'whitespace runs, trimmed'. `FS="[ ]"` means one literal space — and that DOES produce empty fields.

lines: awk '{print $2}'   # an action alone runs on all

items: `BEGIN{}` runs before input: set FS, OFS, print headers
`END{}` runs after the last record: print totals
`awk 'BEGIN{...}'` with no input is a standalone calculator
OFS separates print arguments, ORS ends each record
`print a, b` uses OFS; `print a b` concatenates with nothing

lines: # assigning to a field rebuilds $0 using OFS

items: `RS` sets the record separator, not just the field one
`RS=""` is paragraph mode: blank-line-separated records
`RS=";"` splits on semicolons; gawk allows a regex RS
`$NF` is the last field, `$(NF-1)` the second-to-last
`$x` with a variable is legal: `awk -v c=3 '{print $c}'`

blocks.title: Never Interpolate Shell Vars
blocks.text: Pass values in with `-v var=value` (visible in BEGIN) or `var=value` between filenames (visible once that file starts). Splicing into program text is a quoting bug waiting to happen.

caption.text: Most people learn grep, sed and awk as three unrelated spells — and then spend years debugging the same four silent corruptions. This handbook teaches them as one system: lines, fields, and filters joined by pipes, with the BRE/ERE inversion, the sed cycle, awk's strnum rule, and why `sort -k2` almost never means what you think. 10 pages, no filler — the version I wish someone had handed me before my first 500 GB log.
